title: No room (Luke 2:1–7)
hook: a census, a long walk, a full inn, and a child laid in a feeding trough

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph's dream: a just man who chose gentleness and stayed. Your line was: the one who says nothing and stays. What faithful thing did you do? Day twenty-five.
screen: `THE ONE WHO SAYS NOTHING AND STAYS.`

segments.voice: It starts with paperwork. Luke says an order came down from the emperor in Rome, Caesar Augustus: the whole world was to be enrolled. A census. Taxes. Nobody in Nazareth got a vote. So Joseph has to go to Bethlehem, his family's town, the town of King David, and Mary goes with him, very pregnant, on a trip of about ninety miles. When they arrive, the town is packed. Everyone's come home to be counted. And the baby won't wait. Today, the birth of Jesus, told the way Luke tells it, in seven verses, and the three words everyone remembers: no room.
screen: `AN ORDER FROM ROME.` → `NINETY MILES, VERY PREGNANT.` → `THE TOWN IS PACKED.`

segments.voice: Here's how Luke says it, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him up in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." That's all. No drama, no description of the night. A manger is a feeding trough for animals. So the first bed of the one Catholics call the Son of God is the place where the donkeys eat. Now, a surprise about the word inn. Luke's Greek word, kataluma, is the same word he uses later for the upstairs room where Jesus eats the Last Supper, from day five. So many scholars think it means a guest room in a family house, not a hotel with a grumpy innkeeper. In village homes of that time, the family often lived on a raised floor, and the animals were brought in at night, just below, with the feeding troughs. If the guest room was full, the baby went down by the animals. There's no innkeeper in Luke at all. The Christmas plays added him. Either way, the point holds. The Catholic word for what happened is the Incarnation: God becoming flesh, a real human baby who needed feeding and changing. And he doesn't arrive in a palace, or even a proper room. He arrives in the smallest, lowest space available, among the animals. Remember the Magnificat: the lowly lifted. Here's God choosing the low place himself. Twelve centuries later, Francis of Assisi, from day eight, set up a real manger with a real ox and donkey in a cave at Greccio, so people could see how poor it was. That's where the Christmas crib scene comes from. Every nativity set on every mantel goes back to that night.
screen: `LAID IN A MANGER.` · `KATALUMA — A GUEST ROOM, NOT A HOTEL.` · `GOD BECOMES A BABY.` · `FRANCIS'S MANGER AT GRECCIO.` · then, large: `HE CHOSE THE SMALLEST ROOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice for today's two-minute sit. Think about who has no room today. Someone sleeping in a doorway you pass. A family in a shelter. Someone new at work who doesn't have a seat at the table. A relative nobody invites anymore. Let one of them come to mind, and let them stay there for the whole sit. Don't solve it. Just make room for them in your mind. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
No room. The birth in Bethlehem: a census, a full house, and a baby laid in a feeding trough, God choosing the low place.
Your line: he chose the smallest room. Today, notice who has no room, and make a little: a seat, a spot in the conversation, an invitation. Day twenty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the birth of Jesus at Christmas, with Mass at midnight and on Christmas Day, and many families and parishes set up a nativity scene, a custom traced to Francis of Assisi at Greccio in 1223.

original.note: Greek: a lodging, a guest room. the same word Luke uses for the room of the Last Supper.

trapdoor: what you thought: a mean innkeeper and a stable out back.
what it means: a full house, a baby laid among the animals, and God choosing the lowest place.
what a scholar hears: kataluma, a guest room (Luke 22:11), not pandocheion, the inn of the Good Samaritan; the census under Quirinius is a well-known dating puzzle.

notes: Luke 2:7 quoted from Douay-Rheims; confirm exact wording.
Distance Nazareth–Bethlehem 'about ninety miles' (roughly 70 miles direct, 90 or more by the usual route). Confirm.
Kataluma as guest room and the village-house layout is a widely held modern reading (e.g. Kenneth Bailey), not universal. Presented as 'many scholars think'. Confirm.
Census of Quirinius dating problem mentioned only in the trapdoor; confirm framing.
The script does not date the birth or say 'stable' or 'cave'; the Church of the Nativity tradition (a cave) is omitted. Confirm.
